fix.digest: Marshe noted that five tables were laid, with the twenty-four invited chiefs at two of them; they used no forks and seemed hugely pleased with the feast. When the company gave three huzzas after the naming, the noise startled them. When the deed was brought out, the Oneida leader Shikellamy objected to signing, which Marshe blamed on underhanded dealing by Pennsylvania; the minutes record fourteen chiefs signing that afternoon and the rest on 2 July.

Franklin's 9 May 1753 letter to Collinson (text reprinted by Teaching American History) already contains a counter-offer: the Indians proposed that the English send 'a dozen or two of their Children to Onondago'. The letter names neither Virginia nor Lancaster, and its content can now be described directly.

fix.digest: Writing to Peter Collinson, Franklin told of a treaty between one of the colonies and the Six Nations at which the commissioners offered to educate half a dozen of the Haudenosaunee's brightest boys at a college. In his telling the deputies declined, saying former students had come home good for nothing, and countered that the English should send a dozen or two of their own children to Onondaga to be educated. He names neither Virginia nor Lancaster; the editors of his papers note that this and the 1784 version both differ from the official record.
